Under this proposed Indo-European analysis, compare Old Irish talam (“earth”), Lithuanian Lithuanian tilės and pã-talas (“flooring; bed”), Old Prussian talus (“floor”), Old Church Slavonic т

From eastern Norwegian dialects, from Old Norse greiða, from Proto-Germanic *garaidijaną (“to make ready”). Doublet of greie (“to be able”).
Further discussion
Although gre looks as though it were the Dano-Norwegian form corresponding to native greie, this is actually not the case. The etymon is so marginal in Danish (if in fact it exists at all) that it can be ruled out as the source. Rather, gre was backformed form the past forms gredde, gredd, themselves by pre-cluster shortening from greidde, greidd. There are still certain Norwegian dialects with -ei- in the present and -e- in the past fo

en.g: Titan; the largest moon of Saturn and the second-largest moon in the Solar System, discovered by Christiaan Huygens in 1655
x: The Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005.
Titan er en av Saturns måner.
Titan is one of Saturn's moons.

1000536.etyen:
Internationalism, borrowed from Latin Tītān (“Titan”), from Ancient Greek Τῑτᾱ́ν (Tītā́n, “Titan”), the name of one of the Titans in Greek mythology. The deeper origin of the Ancient Greek name is uncertain; proposed explanations have connected it with τίτο (títo, “sun, day”), τιταίνω (titaínō, “to stretch, extend”) or τίσις (tísis, “retribution”).
The moon was discovered by Christiaan Huygens in 1655. Its present name was proposed by John Herschel in 1847 as part of his naming scheme for Saturn's moons; Herschel chose Titan for Huygens's moon because of its exceptional size.
Compare the paral

1001304.etyen:
First attested before 2000. A distinguishing formation combining Kongo (“Congo”) with the name of the country's capital, Kinshasa, used to distinguish the country from Kongo-Brazzaville (“Congo-Brazzaville”). The formation became possible after the capital, formerly called Léopoldville, was renamed Kinshasa in 1966. The country itself was called Zaïre (“Zaire”) from 1971 to 1997, after which Kongo-Kinshasa returned to use as a distinguishing name.
For the further origin of Kongo, see that entry. The name Kinshasa was taken from the name of an older village at the site of the modern city.

1004632.etyen:
From sviger- (“in-law; denoting a family relationship created through marriage or cohabitation”) + bestemor (“grandmother”), literally “grandmother-in-law”. The combining form sviger- was borrowed from German schwieger- (“in-law”), ultimately from the older noun Schwieger (“mother-in-law”).
Compare Danish svigerbedstemor and Swedish svärmormor (“grandmother-in-law”).

et bådskur med en optrukken båd

1005144.etyen:
Compound of båt (“boat”) + skur (“shed”), literally “boat shed”.
The first element continues Old Norse bátr (“boat”), whose earlier origin is uncertain. NAOB considers possible borrowing from Old English bāt (“boat”) or Old Frisian *bāt (“boat”), as well as a native origin.
The second element shares its origin with Old Norse skúr (“skin around an almond kernel”), belonging to a Proto-Germanic family of words for coverings and shelters, also represented by Old High German scūr (“shelter, shed”). Its more remote derivation is disputed.
Compare the parallel formation Danish bådskur (“boatshed”).
